opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the core reason is that reinforcement learning doesn't need humans to show it the answer. So much of modern machine learning is fundamentally about imitation: you collect a big dataset of what people have done or written, and you train a model to reproduce it. That's incredibly powerful, but it puts a kind of ceiling on things. You're learning to approximate the distribution of human behavior, and if the problem you care about is one where humans don't actually know the answer, imitation alone can only get you so far.

With reinforcement learning, what you need instead is a way to *evaluate* outcomes. You need some signal that says "that was good" or "that was bad," and then the system can explore, try things no one has tried before, and gradually discover strategies that work. Evaluating a solution is often much easier than producing one. In a game, you know whether you won or lost. In a lot of scientific settings, you can measure whether a molecule binds, or whether a design meets some specification, even if nobody knows how to construct the ideal one from first principles.

That's what we saw in the games work over the years. With systems like AlphaGo, and the multi-agent work we did on things like Capture the Flag and StarCraft, the agents would find behaviors that were genuinely surprising, things expert humans hadn't thought of or had dismissed. Once the agent has a learning signal and room to explore, it isn't bound by our priors.

And I think the really exciting part is that you can combine the two. You can use the huge amount of human knowledge we've accumulated as a starting point, a pre-trained model that already understands a lot about the world, and then use reinforcement learning to push beyond it, toward things we don't know yet. For me that's the most promising route to AI that doesn't just automate what we can already do, but actually expands what's possible, particularly in science, in areas like drug discovery, where the space of possibilities is vast and our own intuitions only cover a tiny corner of it.

r001.rationale: The response says RL needs an evaluation signal for whether outcomes are good or bad, allowing exploration even when humans do not know the answer in advance.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, if you look at where the biggest step changes have come from in AI over the last decade, a lot of them trace back to reinforcement learning, and specifically to systems that got to learn from their own experience rather than only from what humans had already written down.

Supervised learning, and really most of what underlies large language models, is fundamentally about imitation. You're compressing the distribution of human output. That gets you something remarkably capable, but it has a ceiling built into it, because the training signal is "what would a person have said or done here." If the thing you care about is beyond what people currently know how to do, there's no data for it. Nobody has written the textbook yet.

Reinforcement learning changes the question. Instead of asking the model to match a human, you ask it to achieve an outcome, and you give it a signal for whether it got there. That's a very different kind of supervision. The agent can try things no human would have thought to try, get feedback from the environment, and push past the human frontier because nothing in the setup anchors it to that frontier.

AlphaGo is the canonical example. The version that learned from human games was strong. The version that learned purely from self-play, with no human data at all, was stronger, and it played moves that professionals initially thought were mistakes and then realised were discoveries. That's the thing I find compelling. The system wasn't just faster at what we already knew. It expanded what was known.

Now, the honest caveat is that this only works when you have a good environment and a reliable reward. Games are easy in that sense. The rules are the simulator and the win condition is the reward. The interesting challenge, and the reason I've spent the last several years in drug discovery, is that a lot of the problems we'd most like to solve beyond human performance, in biology and chemistry and materials, don't come with that for free. The feedback loop is slow, noisy, and expensive. Part of the work is building the environments, learned models of the world that are accurate enough that an agent can learn in them and have that transfer back to reality.

But once you have that loop, even a partial one, you're no longer limited by human intuition about the problem. You're limited by how much experience the agent can gather and how good the signal is. And those are things you can scale. That's what makes it a tool for going beyond us, rather than a better way of catching up to us.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts matching human-provided answers with pursuing an outcome and receiving feedback on whether it was achieved, so correct answers need not be known in advance.

astra-6.text:
I think the exciting thing about reinforcement learning is that it gives you a way to learn from experience, rather than only from examples of what humans have already done. You try something, you observe the outcome, and you use that feedback to improve. If you can do that at scale, you have a mechanism for discovering strategies that we wouldn’t have known to demonstrate in the first place.

That’s particularly compelling in science. We don’t necessarily know what the best molecule looks like or how to solve a particular problem, but we may be able to test a candidate and measure how well it works. That ability to evaluate something can become a learning signal, even when we can’t provide the answer ourselves.

Of course, the hard part is making that loop work: getting reliable feedback, exploring efficiently, and making sure the thing you’re optimizing actually captures what you care about. But that’s why reinforcement learning is so promising. Human knowledge can give you a starting point, and experience can take you beyond it.

r001.rationale: The response explains that a candidate can be tested and its performance measured, providing a learning signal even when humans cannot supply the answer themselves.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the exciting thing about reinforcement learning is that it gives us a way to learn through experience, rather than only learning from examples of what humans have already done. You have a system that takes actions, observes the consequences, and improves according to some measure of success. If you can set that up well, there’s no requirement that a human already knows the best answer.

Games are a really nice illustration of this. You can specify the rules and what it means to win without specifying how to play. Through exploration, a system can discover strategies that we wouldn’t have thought to teach it. And that’s the opportunity in other domains as well: can we define an objective and create an environment where the system can experiment and get useful feedback?

Of course, that’s also the hard part. In science or the real world, experiments can be expensive, feedback can be delayed, and the objective can be difficult to capture. But the underlying idea is powerful: we can potentially discover new knowledge by optimizing for outcomes, rather than being limited to reproducing existing human knowledge.

r001.rationale: The response says reinforcement learning improves by taking actions, observing consequences, and optimizing a success measure, without requiring humans to know the best answer in advance. This communicates learning from evaluations without known correct answers.
